questions.q: Write the formula for the determinant of a 2×2 matrix A = [[a, b], [c, d]] and state the condition under which this matrix is singular.
questions.a: Correct answer: det(A) = ad − bc. The matrix is singular iff ad − bc = 0. A wrong answer (e.g., writing bc − ad, or saying singular when det ≠ 0) reveals confusion between the order of subtraction in the cross-multiplication rule or misunderstanding that singular means determinant zero — both are critical for later inverse matrix work.

questions.q: A student computes the determinant of [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]] by expanding along the first row and gets 0. Another student expands along the second column and gets 18. Without computing, explain why one of them must be wrong and which property of determinants this illustrates.
questions.a: The determinant is unique regardless of expansion row/column — this is the invariance property. The first student is correct (rows are linearly dependent: R3 = 2R2 − R1, so det = 0). The second student made a sign or arithmetic error. A wrong answer shows the student does not grasp that expansion along any row/column yields the same value, which is foundational for strategic choice of expansion line.

questions.q:
Evaluate the determinant: 
| 2  −1  3 |
| 0   4 −2 |
| 1   0  5 |
Show all steps, choosing the expansion that minimises computation.
questions.a:
Optimal expansion: along column 1 (has a zero). 
det = 2 × (+1) × |4 −2; 0 5| + 0 × (...) + 1 × (−1)³⁺¹ × |−1 3; 4 −2|
= 2 × (4×5 − (−2)×0) + 1 × ( (−1)(−2) − 3×4 )
= 2 × 20 + 1 × (2 − 12)
= 40 − 10 = 30.
A wrong answer (e.g., 50 or −30) typically comes from sign errors on the third term (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ or arithmetic in the 2×2 minors.

questions.q: Compare the computational effort of expanding the 3×3 determinant | 1 2 3; 0 4 5; 0 0 6 | along (a) first row, (b) first column, (c) third row. Which is most efficient and why? Generalise the pattern for triangular matrices.
questions.a: (a) First row: three 2×2 minors to compute. (b) First column: only one non-zero entry (1), its minor is |4 5; 0 6| = 24, det = 1×24 = 24. (c) Third row: two zeros, one non-zero (6), minor is |1 2; 0 4| = 4, det = 6×4 = 24. First column and third row are equally efficient (one 2×2 minor). For any triangular matrix (upper or lower), the determinant is the product of diagonal entries — expanding along the first column (lower triangular) or last row (upper triangular) exploits the zeros. Wrong analysis indicates the student cannot recognise structural zeros to reduce work.

questions.q: A student claims: "If I multiply every entry of a 3×3 matrix by 2, the determinant also gets multiplied by 2." Evaluate this claim with a counterexample or proof.
questions.a: The claim is false. If A is 3×3 and B = 2A, then det(B) = 2³ det(A) = 8 det(A), not 2 det(A). Counterexample: A = I₃, det(A) = 1. B = 2I₃ = diag(2,2,2), det(B) = 8. The student confused scalar multiplication of a matrix (each entry × k) with multiplying one row by k (which multiplies det by k). This misconception leads to errors in property applications later.

questions.q: Construct a 3×3 matrix with integer entries between −5 and 5 such that its determinant is exactly 12. Explain your strategy.
questions.a: Strategy: Start with a diagonal matrix diag(3, 2, 2) → det = 12. Or upper triangular with diagonal (3, 2, 2) and arbitrary entries above. Example: [[3, 1, −2], [0, 2, 4], [0, 0, 2]]. Check: expansion along first column gives 3 × |2 4; 0 2| = 3 × 4 = 12. A poor answer (random guessing, or giving a matrix with det ≠ 12) shows inability to use triangular structure to control determinant value — a skill needed for constructing examples in competitive exams.
